context:
It is often said that a translation must choose between fidelity and beauty, as if the two pulled in opposite directions and the translator's only freedom lay in deciding which to betray. The saying flatters our suspicion of translators, but it rests on a confusion about what a text is.

A poem is not a sequence of meanings with a decorative surface laid over them. Its rhythm, its puns, the way a line delays its verb until the reader is nearly out of breath: these are part of what the poem says. A version that preserves every dictionary sense of every word while flattening the rhythm has not been faithful at the expense of beauty; it has been unfaithful in a different place. Fidelity, properly understood, is a property not of words but of effects.

This is not a licence for the translator to do as she pleases. Effects can be specified and argued over, and a translator who turns a mournful poem jaunty has failed by any standard. But it does mean that the familiar charge against "free" translations is often backwards. The translator who renders a joke in the original with a different joke in the new language may be more faithful than the one who renders it word for word and appends a footnote explaining why it was funny.

The real limit, then, lies not between fidelity and beauty but between the effects a language can reproduce and those it cannot. Some losses are unavoidable. The honest translator does not pretend otherwise; she chooses, deliberately and visibly, which losses to accept.
prompt: Does the author hold that any departure from the literal sense of the original is a failure of fidelity?
rationale: The author argues a substituted joke may be more faithful than a literal rendering.

context:
A large observational study followed forty thousand adults for ten years and found that those who reported drinking three or more cups of coffee a day were about fifteen percent less likely to die during the study period than those who drank none. Headlines announced that coffee extends life.

The study's authors were more cautious, and with reason. People who drink a lot of coffee are not a random sample of the population. In earlier decades heavy coffee drinkers were also more likely to smoke, which once made coffee itself look dangerous; the authors therefore adjusted their analysis for smoking, as well as for age, income and exercise. The association survived these adjustments. But adjustment can only remove the influence of factors that were measured, and measured accurately. If, for example, people who are already seriously ill tend to give up coffee on their doctors' advice, then the non-drinkers will include a disproportionate number of sick people, and coffee will appear protective even if it does nothing at all.

One way to probe this possibility is to exclude deaths that occur in the first few years of follow-up, when illness already present at the start of the study is most likely to matter. The authors did so, and the association weakened but did not disappear.

None of this proves that coffee is beneficial. It does suggest that if coffee causes serious harm, the harm is not large enough to show up in a study of this size. That is a more modest conclusion than the headlines, but it is the one the evidence supports.
prompt: Does the author treat the result of excluding early deaths as showing that sick people giving up coffee fully explains the association?
rationale: The association weakened but did not disappear, so that explanation is not treated as complete.

context:
My father kept every map he ever bought. They lived in a drawer in the hall, folded wrong, so that opening one was like wrestling a gull. When I was small he would spread them on the kitchen table and trace routes we never took: the coast road north, a pass through mountains whose names he pronounced with relish and incorrectly. My mother, washing up, would ask where we were going this time, and he would say "Nowhere yet," which I took for years to be the name of a town.

We did not travel much. There was never quite enough money, and later there was never quite enough time, and later still there was his knee. The maps went on accumulating. He bought them in secondhand shops, at stations, once from a man on a ferry who was using one to wrap fish.

After the funeral my brother wanted to throw them out. "He never went anywhere," he said, not unkindly, as if reporting the weather. I did not argue. I took the drawer home, maps and all, and it sits in my own hall now, still stiff, still impossible to close.

Sometimes my daughter pulls one out and asks where we are going. I tell her nowhere yet. She has begun, I notice, to say it the way he did: the slight lift at the end, as if the phrase were not a refusal but a place one might still arrive.
prompt: Does the passage suggest that the daughter's way of saying "nowhere yet" echoes the father's?
rationale: She says it the way he did, with the same lift at the end.

context:
Historians once credited the printing press with the Reformation almost single-handedly: without cheap pamphlets, the argument ran, Luther's protest would have stayed a quarrel among theologians. The claim has the appeal of a clean mechanism, and it is not wrong so much as incomplete.

Print did make a difference. Luther's writings circulated in hundreds of thousands of copies within a few years, and earlier reformers who lacked presses were more easily silenced. But a pamphlet does nothing on a shelf. In a society where most people could not read, printed arguments reached the majority through sermons, readings aloud in taverns and marketplaces, woodcut images and songs. The press multiplied texts; it was older habits of speech and gathering that turned texts into conversations.

There is a further difficulty. Printers were businesses, and they printed what sold. Luther sold. It is at least as plausible to say that the Reformation made the fortunes of German printers as that the printers made the Reformation. Cause and effect ran in both directions, and an account that picks one direction mistakes a feedback loop for a lever.

None of this makes the press irrelevant. It means that asking whether the press "caused" the Reformation is like asking whether the wind or the dry grass caused the fire. The more useful question is how the two interacted, and why the same technology, available elsewhere in Europe, did not everywhere produce the same result.
prompt: Does the author's final sentence suggest that the press by itself cannot explain why the Reformation took hold where it did?
rationale: If the same technology elsewhere produced different results, other factors must matter.

context:
A student hypothesized that a particular soil fungus helps tomato seedlings survive drought. She grew forty seedlings in sterilized soil, inoculated twenty of them with the fungus, and withheld water from all forty for twelve days. At the end, seventeen of the inoculated plants were alive, compared with nine of the uninoculated ones.

Her teacher raised two questions. The first was whether the plants had been assigned to the two groups at random. They had not: the student had inoculated the twenty seedlings on the sunnier side of the greenhouse bench, because that tray was closer to where she worked. Since sunlight affects both growth and water loss, the teacher pointed out, the experiment could not separate the effect of the fungus from the effect of position.

The second question concerned the inoculation itself. To introduce the fungus, the student had mixed a spoonful of fungal culture, grown on a nutrient medium, into the soil of each treated pot. The untreated pots received nothing. Thus the treated plants had received not only the fungus but also whatever nutrients remained in the culture medium.

The student repeated the experiment. This time she numbered the pots, used a random-number table to choose which twenty would be inoculated, and added to each untreated pot a spoonful of the same medium that had been sterilized by heat. The difference in survival was smaller than before but still clear: fifteen of the inoculated seedlings survived, against ten of the controls.
prompt: In the second experiment, was the sterilized medium added to the untreated pots meant to address the teacher's concern about position on the bench?
rationale: Random assignment addressed position; the sterilized medium addressed the extra-nutrients confound.
